days.note: A fishing town turns 100, and the fog that rolls in brings back what the town owes. John Carpenter's follow-up to Halloween.
Five friends, a cabin, and a tape recorder that should never have been played. Sam Raimi, shot for almost nothing.
A TV reporter goes away to recover, and the other guests are werewolves. Rob Bottin's transformation is still astonishing.
An Antarctic research station, twelve men, and something that can become any of them.
Stephen King and George A. Romero's comic-book anthology: five stories, one with King himself turning into a lawn.
A medical student with a glowing green serum and no sense of when to stop. Lovecraft by way of splatter comedy.
A quiet seaside town where visitors are killed, then turn up again, friendly as ever.
Something is living under New York and coming up through the manholes. Cannibalistic Humanoid Underground Dwellers.
A baby alligator flushed down the toilet grows up in the Chicago sewers. Written by John Sayles.
Two kids find a hole in the backyard that leads somewhere it shouldn't. The effects are all tricks of the camera.
A family's new satellite dish picks up an alien that eats whoever it sees. Gloriously garish.
Sonny Bono, a young Julia Louis-Dreyfus, a boy called Harry Potter, and a troll taking over a San Francisco apartment building, one flat at a time.
Teenagers locked in a shopping mall overnight with three security robots that have stopped taking orders.
A circus tent lands outside town, and the clowns inside wrap their victims in cotton candy.
Say his name above a whisper and Madman Marz comes. A campfire story told straight, in the woods, at night.
Three children born during an eclipse turn ten, and start killing. The killer-kids film people forget.
A beach-house weekend with a father who never got over an accident. Originally called Fall Break; the effects are the star.
Cannon goes punk: a TV countdown show, and a caller promising a murder at every midnight.
Susan Tyrrell as the aunt who will not let her nephew grow up. The most unhinged performance of the decade.
Linnea Quigley, a bowling alley after hours, and an imp who grants wishes badly. The midweek palate cleanser.
A theatre troupe locked in overnight with a killer in an owl mask. Michele Soavi's debut, and the best slasher of the late 80s.
A funeral in the English countryside, and a sister-in-law with a coven. José Ramón Larraz at his most lurid.
A young solicitor settles a dead woman's affairs in a house cut off by the tide. Nigel Kneale's TV film, and the quietest, most frightening night of the month.
A marriage in West Berlin comes apart, and what replaces it waits in a locked apartment. Isabelle Adjani has no equal here.
A salaryman starts turning into scrap metal. Sixty-seven minutes of Tokyo industrial nightmare.
A bookshop clerk reads a pulp novel, and its killer walks off the page. From the director of The Gate.
A witch-hunter follows a warlock from 1691 to modern Los Angeles. Julian Sands is very good at being very bad.
Two LA cops, one of them already dead, chase a gang that won't stay down.
Aliens harvest a New Zealand town for their fast-food chain. Peter Jackson's first film, made on weekends with friends.
A haunted mansion, a sorcerer, and a monster for every guest. Famously two films stitched into one.
Halloween night: punks, a cemetery and "Party Time". Zombies that want brains, and say so.
